title: A bigger MOQ on one grinder starves its sister SKU
brief: The Warsaw DC holds 14 weeks of stock for SKU G-110 (coffee grinder) while sister SKU G-120 is stocked out with backorders. Planners want to know why and what to do.

evidence.content: G-110 on hand 4,200 units (about 14 weeks of cover). G-120 on hand 0 with 600 units backordered.
From 1 Sep the supplier raised the MOQ for G-110 from 500 to 3,000 units. The G-120 MOQ is unchanged at 500.
G-110 demand is stable at about 300 units/week; G-120 demand is about 400 units/week, up 10%.
G-110 and G-120 are built on the same production line. G-120 PO 6120 (2,000 units) was delayed 3 weeks because the line first ran the 3,000-unit G-110 batch.
All inbound shipments arrived as planned; no transport delays.
The G-120 reorder point was lowered from 800 to 700 units in August.

answer_key.root_cause: The MOQ increase on G-110 forced a 3,000-unit batch on the production line shared with G-120, which pushed G-120's PO 6120 back three weeks: overstock on G-110, stock-out on G-120.

remediation_rubric.criterion: Expedite G-120 (partial shipment / priority on the line)
Negotiate the G-110 MOQ or batch sequencing with the supplier
Adjust ordering: hold G-110 orders, prioritise G-120 allocation
Consider a second source for G-120
Make shared-capacity constraints visible in planning

answer_key.notes: E6 is a small, real change but not the cause.

registry.mechanism_opportunities: Supplier contract detail (E2) matters to Inventory, which can't predict that. V2 may hide it; V1 Supplier -> Inventory path helps.
